triage_risk_rating.rationale: Initiation is Medium because the alert shows internal IP-to-IP network activity with no payload, port, or protocol context; occurrence is High because there are 80 alerts with a risk score of 70 indicating repeated detection; adverse impact is Medium because the IOC match suggests anomalous communication but there is no evidence of PowerShell, endpoint, file, or web malicious activity.

incident_details.title: High Risk Alerts: ESA for 192.168.0.34
incident_details.description: This is a high-severity network-only alert showing internal host 192.168.0.34 communicating with internal host 192.168.0.19, with no protocol or destination port context available. There is no evidence of PowerShell or other endpoint execution artifacts, so the activity is suspicious but unverified rather than confirmed malicious behavior.

requested_gaps: step_2: Was it horizontal or vertical
step_3: Was any malicious process spawned on the victim's machine?
step_4: Analyze the process tree for signs of malicious activity, such as privilege escalation, lateral movement, or data exfiltration.
step_1: Identify 1. username 2. IP address 3. Login Details 4. Computer name 5. Operating System

gap_findings.step_1: The incident data provides only network-level alert metadata and does not include a username, login session details, computer name, or operating system. The only concrete host identity clue is the source IP 192.168.0.34 and destination IP 192.168.0.19, which suggests activity within the same 192.168.0.0/24 network. No authentication, endpoint, or asset inventory fields are present, so user identity and OS cannot be determined from this dataset.
gap_findings.step_2: The available IPs indicate likely horizontal movement if the source host 192.168.0.34 was interacting with 192.168.0.19 on the same /24 subnet, because same-subnet activity is more consistent with peer-to-peer or lateral communication than a subnet-hop into a different network. However, there is no port, protocol, authentication, or endpoint process evidence to prove lateral movement versus routine east-west traffic, so this remains an inference rather than a confirmed movement type.
gap_findings.step_3: No process information is present in the incident data. There are no process names, parent-child relationships, command lines, hashes, service creation indicators, or execution events that would show whether a malicious process spawned on the victim machine.
gap_findings.step_4: A process tree cannot be analyzed from the current data because no process telemetry exists in the incident payload. Therefore there is no evidence here of privilege escalation, lateral movement through spawned binaries, credential dumping, or exfiltration tooling. The alert is only identified as a high-risk event stream alert tied to IP communication, so any malicious process-chain reasoning would require endpoint telemetry.

actionable_queries.step_1: Query Windows Security Event Log for Event ID 4624 and 4625 on host 192.168.0.34 and 192.168.0.19; correlate with EDR device inventory to map IP-to-hostname, logged-on user, logon type, and OS version. If available, query AD/EDR asset inventory for device.name, user.name, and operatingSystem for those IPs.
actionable_queries.step_2: Check Windows Security Logs and firewall/EDR network telemetry for connections between 192.168.0.34 and 192.168.0.19; use netstat -ano or EDR network connection search to identify whether the destination was a peer host on the same subnet. Correlate with Event ID 4648/4624/4672 on both hosts to determine whether movement was authenticated lateral access.
actionable_queries.step_3: Pull EDR process-creation telemetry or Windows Security Event ID 4688, Sysmon Event ID 1, and PowerShell logs (Event ID 4104) for the relevant time window on the victim host. Search for suspicious parent-child chains, especially explorer.exe -> cmd.exe/powershell.exe/wmic.exe/rundll32.exe/schtasks.exe/mshta.exe/regsvr32.exe.
actionable_queries.step_4: Collect full process tree telemetry from EDR, Sysmon Event ID 1, and optional Sysmon Event IDs 3, 7, 10, 11, 12, 13, 22 to look for network connections, image loads, process access, file creation, registry persistence, and DNS activity. If privilege escalation is suspected, query Event IDs 4672, 4688, 7045, and 4697; if data exfiltration is suspected, review outbound connections and large file transfer events on the endpoint and proxy logs.

triage_deep_dive.deep_dive_summary: This incident contains only high-risk event-stream network metadata: source 192.168.0.34 communicating with destination 192.168.0.19 on the same /24 subnet. That supports a possible horizontal/lateral movement hypothesis, but there is no endpoint telemetry, process tree, user, hostname, or OS evidence to confirm malicious execution or privilege escalation. Additional Windows security, Sysmon, and EDR process/network logs are required to resolve the gaps.
